result: Genetic disruption of V-ATPase subunits stabilizes HIF1α in aerobic conditions. A forward genetic screen identified five V-ATPase subunits (ATP6AP1, ATP6V1A, ATP6V1G1, ATP6V0A2, ATP6V0D1) enriched for gene-trapping insertions. CRISPR-Cas9 depletion of these subunits and chemical inhibition with Bafilomycin A both increased HIF1α levels without affecting HIF1α mRNA expression.
evaluation: Claims C1, C18, C22-C26 provide converging evidence from an unbiased genetic screen, CRISPR validation, and pharmacological inhibition. The genetic screen data (Figure 1A-C), CRISPR-Cas9 experiments (Figure 1D-E), and BafA treatment (Figure 1F-G) all demonstrate HIF1α stabilization. The lack of effect on mRNA levels (C27, Figure 9J) supports post-translational regulation.

result: TMEM199 and CCDC115 are mammalian V-ATPase assembly factors that stabilize HIF1α when disrupted. TMEM199 shows 24% sequence identity to yeast Vma12p, and CCDC115 shows structural homology to yeast Vma22p. Both proteins associate with V-ATPase subunits, and their depletion stabilizes HIF1α similarly to V-ATPase subunit depletion.
evaluation: Claims C2, C19, C20, C28-C32, C34-C35, C37-C38, C40-C41 are well-supported by genetic screen data (Figure 2A), sequence homology analysis (Figure 2B), CRISPR validation with rescue experiments (Figures 2C-F), mass spectrometry (Figure 2G), structural prediction (Figure 2H), and co-immunoprecipitation (Figure 2I). The rescue experiments (C32, C35) provide strong evidence for specificity.

result: TMEM199 and CCDC115 localize to the endoplasmic reticulum and form a complex analogous to yeast Vma12p-Vma22p. TMEM199 is present only in membrane fractions and localizes predominantly to the ER. CCDC115 co-localizes with TMEM199 at the ER, though it is mostly cytosolic.
evaluation: Claims C42-C46 are supported by cell fractionation (Figure 3A), immunofluorescence microscopy with quantitative colocalization analysis (Figures 3B-E), and comparison to yeast studies (C42). The ER localization is consistent with a role in V-ATPase assembly rather than function in mature complexes.

result: TMEM199 and CCDC115 are required for V-ATPase-dependent lysosomal degradation and endosomal acidification. Depletion of TMEM199 or CCDC115 prevents EGFR degradation and MHC Class I degradation similarly to BafA treatment. Live cell microscopy with pH-sensitive transferrin receptor demonstrates that depletion of these proteins prevents endosomal acidification.
evaluation: Claims C47-C51 are supported by EGFR degradation assays (Figures 4A-C), MHC Class I rescue experiments (Figure 4D), and live cell microscopy with pH-sensitive Tfnr-phl (Figures 5A-D). The functional assays demonstrate that TMEM199/CCDC115 are required for V-ATPase function in both lysosomal degradation and endosomal acidification.

result: V-ATPase inhibition causes nuclear accumulation of HIF1α sufficient to activate HIF target genes. BafA treatment increases HIF1α levels within 4 hours to levels similar to proteasome inhibition. HIF1α accumulates in the nucleus rather than in endosomal-lysosomal compartments, and this is sufficient to activate HIF responsive genes including CA9, HIF2α, and HO-1.
evaluation: Claims C52-C56 are supported by immunoblot comparisons (Figure 6A), time-course experiments (Figure 6B), immunofluorescence microscopy (Figures 6C-D), and flow cytometry/immunoblot analysis of HIF target genes (Figures 6E-G). The nuclear localization and functional activation of target genes demonstrate that V-ATPase inhibition leads to bona fide HIF pathway activation.

result: V-ATPase inhibition stabilizes HIF1α by preventing prolyl hydroxylation rather than through chaperone-mediated autophagy. Depletion of CMA mediators (HSC70, LAMP2A) or ATG16 has no effect on HIF1α stabilization. V-ATPase inhibitors stabilize non-hydroxylated HIF1α, while proteasome inhibition stabilizes hydroxylated HIF1α. In vitro hydroxylation assays demonstrate that BafA treatment markedly reduces PHD activity.
evaluation: Claims C57-C61 are supported by CRISPR/siRNA depletion experiments (Figures 7A-D), prolyl-hydroxylation-specific immunoblots (Figures 7E-F), and in vitro hydroxylation assays (Figures 7G-H). The data clearly distinguish between proteasomal and lysosomal mechanisms and demonstrate that V-ATPase inhibition impairs PHD enzymatic activity rather than preventing lysosomal degradation.

result: V-ATPase disruption results in intracellular iron depletion. BafA treatment stabilizes IRP2 (a sensitive marker of iron deficiency) similarly to the iron chelator DFO. BafA treatment increases NCOA4 but ferritin levels remain unchanged, consistent with a complete block in autophagy. Genetic disruption of V-ATPase subunits (TMEM199, CCDC115, ATP6V0D1, ATP6V1A1) also increases IRP2 and NCOA4 levels.
evaluation: Claims C3-C4, C68-C72 are supported by immunoblot analysis of iron homeostasis markers (Figures 8A-B). The accumulation of IRP2 provides strong evidence for iron depletion, and the pattern of NCOA4 and ferritin levels is consistent with impaired autophagy. The observation that genetic disruption of multiple V-ATPase components produces the same phenotype strengthens the conclusion.

result: Iron supplementation directly restores PHD activity and HIF1α turnover following V-ATPase inhibition. Addition of 1 μM Fe(II) completely restores in vitro prolyl hydroxylation in BafA-treated lysates. Iron citrate (50-200 μM Fe(III)) prevents HIF1α stabilization and downstream target gene activation in BafA-treated cells across multiple cell types. Iron supplementation reverses HIF1α stabilization in genetic V-ATPase knockouts but has no effect on proteasome inhibition or VHL-null cells.
evaluation: Claims C5, C73-C79, C81 are supported by in vitro hydroxylation assays (Figures 8C-F), flow cytometry and immunoblot analysis (Figures 9A-H), RT-qPCR (Figure 9J), and genetic rescue experiments (Figures 9K-M). The specificity of iron rescue (no effect on MG132 or VHL-null cells) and the dose-response relationship provide strong evidence that iron depletion is the mechanism linking V-ATPase inhibition to HIF1α stabilization.

result: Transferrin-mediated iron uptake is the predominant mechanism for maintaining cytosolic iron levels. Pre-conditioning with iron does not prevent HIF1α accumulation following BafA treatment, but concurrent or subsequent iron supplementation does, suggesting transferrin-independent uptake. NCOA4 depletion has no effect on HIF1α levels, while transferrin receptor or IRP2 depletion stabilizes HIF1α. Iron supplementation restores HIF1α turnover in transferrin receptor-deficient cells.
evaluation: Claims C82-C91 are supported by time-course experiments (Figure 10A), CRISPR depletion studies (Figures 10B-F), and iron rescue experiments (Figures 10G-H). The differential effects of NCOA4 vs. transferrin receptor depletion provide strong evidence for the relative importance of iron uptake vs. ferritin turnover. The ability of extracellular iron to rescue transferrin receptor-deficient cells demonstrates transferrin-independent uptake mechanisms.

result: Background on HIF1α regulation and prior observations on lysosomal inhibitors. HIF1α is constitutively expressed but rapidly degraded by the proteasome following prolyl hydroxylation by PHDs and ubiquitination by VHL. Prior studies reported that lysosomal inhibitors can stabilize HIF1α, with proposed mechanisms including CMA, mitochondrial uncoupling, and V-ATPase-VHL binding.
evaluation: Claims C6-C17 are primarily based on citations to established literature and provide context for the current study. These claims accurately represent prior knowledge and observations, though the current study challenges some of the proposed mechanisms (particularly CMA).

result: Background on V-ATPase function and PHD cofactor requirements. The V-ATPase is required for lysosomal degradation. PHDs require Fe(II) and 2-oxoglutarate as cofactors. The V-ATPase is implicated in iron homeostasis through transferrin endocytosis, ferric-to-ferrous conversion, and ferritin degradation. IRP2 is a sensitive marker of intracellular iron.
evaluation: Claims C21, C62-C67 are based on established knowledge and citations to prior literature. These claims provide essential background for understanding the experimental findings and are accurately represented.

result: Human mutations in V-ATPase components and assembly factors cause diverse diseases. Most TMEM199 knockout clones are lethal. Human mutations in TMEM199 and CCDC115 cause glycosylation defects and liver storage disease. Mutations in V-ATPase subunits cause osteopetrosis and renal acidosis. ATP6AP1 mutations cause immunodeficiency, and VMA21 mutations cause autophagic myopathy.
evaluation: Claims C33, C36, C39, C92-C95, C111-C115 are supported by experimental observations (C33) and citations to clinical literature. These claims provide important context for the physiological relevance of the findings, though they are primarily descriptive rather than mechanistic.

result: Discussion and interpretation of findings. Iron rescue experiments argue against CMA involvement. The major consequence of V-ATPase inhibition is HIF1α stabilization by preventing prolyl hydroxylation. Findings are consistent with prior studies on V-ATPase and iron metabolism. Decreased transferrin uptake is the predominant mechanism. Transferrin-independent iron uptake can occur with sufficient extracellular iron. HIF activation and V-ATPase activity may serve as a feedback mechanism for iron control.
evaluation: Claims C96-C110 represent interpretations and synthesis of the experimental findings. These are generally well-supported by the data presented, though some claims (particularly C107 about feedback mechanisms) are more speculative. The interpretations are logical and consistent with the experimental evidence.

result: Bafilomycin A treatment does not affect HIF1α mRNA expression.
evaluation: Claim C27 is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 9J. This control experiment is important for demonstrating that HIF1α stabilization occurs at the post-translational level.
